Reserve Currencies and Stablecoins Introduction [OFFICIAL] you to the Karl Brunner Institute of Macroeconomic Policy for the kind invitation to speak at the SNB and Its Watchers conference this year. I look forward to a great discussion with Hans, [OFFICIAL], and Carolyn. And thank you to Gianluca for moderating. The role of safe haven currencies in our world economy is always an important topic of discussion. I previously spoke on this in March at the University of [CITY] Booth School of Business’s US Monetary Policy [OFFICIAL].1 Today’s panel—with its focus on stablecoins—provides an intriguing angle through which to discuss evolving dynamics of safe-haven currencies. First, I’ll note that the views I express today are mine and not those of the Federal Reserve System or my colleagues on the Federal Open Market Committee.

The dollar is used in most foreign-exchange transactions, even when Americans aren’t involved. The standard can change, but it doesn’t change quickly. From the mid-19th century until World War I, the British pound was the leading currency for trade, capital investment, and reserves around the world. The pound and the dollar traded the top spot between the world wars, after which the dollar became the leading international currency. Other currencies have played roles, as well. The Japanese yen, while far from internationally dominant, has traditionally been considered a safe-haven currency, owing to Japan’s large international creditor position and its long period of low interest rates. The Swiss franc is also worth discussing given its history and our setting today. It was the sixth-most-traded currency based on foreign exchange transactions in 2025, and it has long been considered a safe-haven currency.

By most measures, the Swiss franc is a model of what investors want in a crisis. Switzerland has strong institutions, a long tradition of political neutrality, low inflation, and a credible central bank. When markets get nervous, money flows in. And yet, central banks hold only a sliver of their reserves in francs—about one fourth of one percent.6 So why the gap? Part of the answer is scale. Switzerland’s economy and its government bond market are small. There aren’t enough safe Swiss franc assets for the world to hold in size. Large safe-haven inflows can easily push up the Swiss franc and squeeze Swiss exporters. So the Swiss National Bank has kept its policy rate at zero and has made clear it’s ready to intervene in currency markets to lean against those inflows.7 In other words, a reserve currency has to be more than trusted.

The Federal Reserve's congressionally assigned dual mandate is to conduct monetary policy in pursuit of maximum employment and price stability. That said, the value of the dollar is one of many factors affecting prices and, overall, the economy, so it’s something I watch. The Federal Reserve also has responsibility for monitoring and promoting financial stability, and the dollar is an important piece in the interconnected global financial system. Delivering on our commitments is an important way the Federal Reserve helps the dollar remain a reliable store of value and that Americans can continue to reap the benefits of its global status. This includes bringing inflation back to our 2 percent goal, sustaining a healthy labor market, and supporting a resilient financial system.

High inflation erodes the purchasing power of dollar cash holdings and nominal bonds. Since I spoke about this topic in early March, inflation has moved in the wrong direction. Headline PCE inflation was 3.6 percent in September, and core PCE inflation was 3.1 percent. Those readings are well above our 2 percent goal and higher than at the start of this year. Inflation has now been above our goal for nearly six years, and the pressures I’m seeing appear to be relatively broad based, reflecting both supply and demand. I expect that monetary policy will need to move to a restrictive stance to bring inflation back to 2 percent in a timely manner. I prefer getting to that stance through more frequent smaller adjustments when possible, something which would be less disruptive to households, businesses, and financial markets.

This strategy would also reduce the risk of having policy fall behind where it needs to be and an inflationary mindset take hold. The Fed’s independence, along with its accountability to Congress, is critical to maintaining the world’s confidence in our commitment to 2 percent inflation. Through its actions, the Fed has earned credibility as an institution that conducts monetary policy based on evidence and economic data rather than on short-term political pressures. That credibility helps us achieve our objectives, including low and stable inflation, while supporting the status of the dollar. Impact of Stablecoins Losing any one of these benefits could diminish the dollar’s status as a reserve currency. But moving away from the dollar would likely require an attractive alternative.

Because stablecoins’ price stability is best achieved by backing them with safe and liquid assets, new money flowing into stablecoins may translate into demand for Treasury bills. Studies tend to agree that US dollar stablecoin inflows have the potential to lower Treasury bill yields, particularly if their size and scale grow significantly.9 While stablecoins have been around since 2014, with new US federal rules taking effect in January, they’re entering a different phase.10 There is an open question about the extent to which stablecoin regulation at the national level, such as the Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for US Stablecoins or GENIUS Act, will affect global demand for US dollars. As this group likely knows, the GENIUS Act was signed into US law in July 2025, establishing a comprehensive national regulatory framework for payment stablecoins and guaranteeing that payment stablecoins can be easily redeemed for dollars.

Of course, stablecoins may have technological advantages over traditional payment methods, such as the ability to execute smart contracts or to enable agentic workflows. These features may raise demand for stablecoins and thus for US dollar assets. However, current US regulation does not directly address use of smart contracts or agentic AI for payments. Without regulatory clarity, US institutions may be slow to adopt these technologies. Conclusion As I noted earlier, the depth of investable assets in US markets is unparalleled. America’s legal system endures as one in which investors can be confident that contracts will be enforced and laws upheld. And with support from an independent Federal Reserve, the nation’s economy and its financial institutions are strong and stable.

The dollar’s status depends on preserving the fundamental qualities that underlie its strength, qualities that provide a solid foundation for any currency. This includes maintaining central bank independence so we can deliver on our mission. As a Federal Reserve policymaker, I’m committed to achieving our price stability and maximum employment objectives on behalf of the American public. [OFFICIAL] you, and I look forward to the discussion.
